issues.legal_issue: Compulsory acquisition of private passenger-transport assets for operation by a public transport body serves a public purpose even when comparable assets are available for purchase in the market.
material_facts: The acquisition covered contract carriages, their permits, and related property for transfer to a public road transport corporation.
The stated objectives included preventing misuse of contract-carriage permits and improving passenger transport facilities.
The legislation contemplated the corporation operating the acquired vehicles as a public transport service.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was for a public purpose; the possibility of purchasing similar assets in the market did not invalidate it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2), whether an acquisition is for a public purpose is justiciable and is determined from the legislation’s objects, preamble, provisions, context, and purpose. Kesavananda Bharati was applied. The Court also referred to State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh. A public purpose may be served by acquisition of movable or immovable property, and the public purpose need not depend on urgency, scarcity, or the unavailability of private purchases. Section 4(3)’s use of “deemed” did not necessarily create a legal fiction; its meaning depended on the statute’s context.

predicates.acquisition_constitutionality_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition.
predicates.assets_taken_for_public_passenger_transp: The government took transport vehicles and associated assets for use in a public passenger-transport service.
predicates.misuse_of_transport_authorizations_was_s: The government sought to prevent operators from using transport authorizations in a manner considered detrimental to the public interest.
predicates.better_public_transport_was_sought: The government sought to improve passenger transport facilities for the public.
predicates.acquisition_serves_a_public_purpose: The acquisition serves a public purpose.

issues.definition: When a challenged acquisition takes transport assets for public passenger transport and is directed at preventing misuse or improving public service, the rule treats it as serving a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: An acquisition-amount framework is not invalid merely because its payment may be inadequate if, properly construed, it provides a non-arbitrary and non-illusory amount determined through a just-and-reasonable assessment.
material_facts: The legislation provided for an arbitrator to determine the amount payable where agreement was not reached.
The arbitrator was required to determine an amount appearing just and reasonable, considering the circumstances and the scheduled guidance so far as applicable.
The legislation provided for an appeal from the arbitrator’s award to the High Court.
The Court construed the schedule as guidance for the arbitrator rather than an inflexible limit on the amount.
issues.conclusion: On the Court’s construction, the amount provisions were not wholly arbitrary or illusory and did not invalidate the law under Article 31(2); inadequacy alone was not a ground for invalidation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as considered in Kesavananda Bharati, does not permit an amount to be wholly arbitrary or illusory, but does not allow a challenge merely because the amount is inadequate. The Court considered State of West Bengal v. Bela Banerjee, P. Vajravelu Mudaliar v. Special Deputy Collector, Union of India v. Metal Corporation of India, State of Gujarat v. Shantilal Mangaldas, and Rustom Cavasjee Cooper v. Union of India in explaining the constitutional history and effect of the Twenty-fifth Amendment. Reading the amount provisions together, the arbitrator must decide what is just and reasonable on the circumstances, keeping the schedule in mind without being bound to apply it as a fixed measure; “having regard to” makes the schedule a guide, not a fetter. Saraswati Industrial Syndicate Ltd. v. Union of India, Illingworth v. Walmsley, and Perry v. Wright were relied on in construing that expression.

predicates.acquisition_amount_challenge: A party challenged the amount payable for property compulsorily taken.
predicates.amount_framework_provides_independent_as: The payment framework authorizes an independent decision-maker to assess the amount payable.
predicates.arbitrator_must_determine_a_just_and_rea: The decision-maker must determine an amount considered just and reasonable in the circumstances.
predicates.amount_is_not_wholly_arbitrary_or_illuso: The amount framework does not produce a wholly arbitrary or illusory return for the property taken.
predicates.amount_framework_is_not_invalid_merely_f: The amount framework is not invalid merely because the amount may be inadequate.

issues.definition: If a challenged acquisition framework requires an independent, just-and-reasonable assessment and is not wholly arbitrary or illusory, inadequacy alone does not make the framework invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The scheduled acquisition cost of a vehicle’s chassis means the purchaser’s price charged by the manufacturer’s dealer, while the acquisition cost of its body means the amount charged by the body builder.
material_facts: The legislation used the expression “acquisition cost” to calculate the amount payable for a vehicle.
The legislation described that cost by reference to the chassis and the vehicle body as charged by their respective suppliers.
The Court construed the chassis cost as the price paid by the purchaser to the manufacturer’s dealer, and the body cost as the actual charge made by the body builder.
issues.conclusion: “Acquisition cost” means the dealer’s price to the purchaser for the chassis and the body builder’s actual charge for the vehicle body, not the manufacturer’s cost of making the chassis.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read the explanation of “acquisition cost” together with the relevant schedule paragraph and adopted a construction consistent with the purchaser’s acquisition price and the body builder’s charge.

predicates.vehicle_acquisition_cost_disputed: A dispute arose about how to calculate a vehicle’s acquisition cost.
predicates.chassis_bought_through_manufacturer_deal: The purchaser obtained the chassis from a dealer selling for the manufacturer.
predicates.vehicle_body_built_by_body_builder: A body builder constructed the vehicle body and charged for that work.
predicates.chassis_cost_is_dealer_price_and_body_co: The chassis cost is the dealer’s price to the purchaser, and the body cost is the body builder’s charge.

issues.definition: For a disputed vehicle acquisition cost, a chassis bought through the manufacturer’s dealer is valued at the purchaser’s dealer price and a body built by a body builder at that builder’s charge.

issues.legal_issue: A state may acquire the in-state operation rights represented by an interstate transport permit, but may not acquire an out-of-state counter-signature portion or a vehicle whose initial permit was granted by another state.
material_facts: The challenged law acquired vehicles and permits connected with transport operators in the state.
Some permits were initially granted by the state and counter-signed by authorities in other states.
Other permits or vehicles were connected to an initial permit granted by another state.
The Court treated the counter-signed portion as a separate permit authorizing operation in the other state and read the law to avoid extra-territorial operation.
issues.conclusion: The law validly reached vehicles kept and registered in the state with permits initially granted there, but did not reach the counter-signed portions authorizing operation elsewhere or vehicles operating on initial permits granted by another state.
issues.legal_principle: The law’s pith and substance was acquisition of transport vehicles, permits, and property situated in the state; incidental encroachment on another legislative field did not invalidate it. The Court relied on Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v. Bank of Commerce, Kerala State Electricity Board v. Indian Aluminium Co., A. S. Krishna v. State of Madras, S. K. Pasari v. Abdul Ghafoor, Narayanappa v. State of Mysore, and Tansukh Rai Jain v. Nilratan Prasad Shaw for legislative competence and incidental encroachment. M/s Bundelkhand Motor Transport Company v. Behari Lal Chaurasia and Punjab Sikh Regular Motor Service v. Regional Transport Authority supported treating an initial permit and its counter-signature as distinct permits. The Court also relied on Bengal Immunity Co. v. State of Bihar, R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India, and Gulabhai Vallabhbhai Desai v. Union of India in reading down the law to avoid extra-territorial operation. The law was in pith and substance one of acquisition, and incidental encroachment did not invalidate it.

rule.if: state_acquisition_law_challenged and interstate_transport_permit_involved and (initial_permit_granted_in_state or out_of_state_countersignature_exists or initial_permit_granted_outside_state)

predicates.state_acquisition_law_challenged: A party challenged a state law authorizing acquisition of transport vehicles or permits.
predicates.interstate_transport_permit_involved: The transport authorization allowed operation across state boundaries.
predicates.initial_permit_granted_in_state: The initial transport permit was granted by an authority in the acquiring state.
predicates.out_of_state_countersignature_exists: An authority in another state added a counter-signature authorizing operation there.
predicates.initial_permit_granted_outside_state: The initial transport permit was granted by an authority outside the acquiring state.
predicates.acquisition_is_limited_to_in_state_permi: The acquisition reaches only the in-state permit rights and does not reach out-of-state permit rights or vehicles based on an initial permit granted elsewhere.

issues.definition: When a challenged state acquisition concerns interstate permits, the acquisition reaches the in-state permit rights but not out-of-state permit rights or vehicles based on an initial permit granted elsewhere.

issues.legal_issue: Nationalisation of private transport assets may constitute distribution of community material resources for the common good and may qualify for constitutional protection when the required connection to that objective exists.
material_facts: The legislation declared an objective of distributing material resources to subserve the common good and preventing concentration of wealth.
It acquired privately operated buses and related assets for transfer to a public transport corporation.
The separate opinion treated private buses as material resources and public-sector nationalisation as a form of distribution.
issues.conclusion: In Justice Krishna Iyer’s separate opinion, the acquisition had the required connection to the constitutional objective of distributing material resources for the common good and qualified for the protection of Article 31C. The other members of the Court did not express agreement with all of that separate opinion and the majority expressly left the issue undecided.
issues.legal_principle: Justice Krishna Iyer applied Article 31C with Article 39(b) and (c), read in light of Article 38 and Kesavananda Bharati. He treated private property as capable of being a material resource of the community and understood distribution to include acquisition from private ownership and allocation to the public sector for the common good. The majority judgment expressly stated that it was unnecessary to decide the issue under Article 31C.

predicates.constitutional_immunity_claimed: A party relied on a constitutional protection for legislation pursuing specified social and economic objectives.
predicates.law_declares_common_good_distribution_ob: The law states that it is directed to distributing material resources for the common good.
predicates.private_transport_assets_allocated_to_pu: Privately owned transport assets are acquired and allocated to a public passenger-transport service.
predicates.separate_opinion_treats_law_as_qualifyin: The separate opinion treats the law as qualifying for the claimed constitutional protection.

issues.definition: When a law declares a common-good distribution objective and allocates privately owned transport assets to public service, the separate opinion treats it as qualifying for constitutional protection.
